newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Korean Air Lines earnings seen unaffected by crash.
newsitem.headline: Korean Air Lines earnings seen unaffected by crash.

text.p: Korean Air Lines is expected to announce huge losses for the first half of calendar 1997, but those losses should narrow for the whole year despite Wednesday's crash of one of its jumbo jets, analysts said.
A Korean Air jumbo jet with 231 passengers and 23 crew members aboard crashed on the Pacific island of Guam early on Wednesday morning. More than 200 people were feared dead.
Shares of Korean Air opened limit-down at 14,900 won ($16.70) when trading began on the Seoul bourse, but later rebounded to 15,500, off 600 from the previous day's close.
Analysts said the crash would damage the credibility and name value of South Korea's flagship airline, but would not substantially impact the company's earnings.
"It will definitely hurt Korean Air's image. I'm worrying about its long-term side-effect," said Park Yoo-kyung, an airline analyst at ING-Barings.

Analysts forecast first-half losses for the company of 150 billion to 220 billion won against a 253.8 billion loss during the same period a year earlier. The company experienced substantial foreign currency translation losses, they said.
Korean Air, an affiliate of South Korea's seventh largest Hanjin Group, was due to release its interim results next week.
Analysts said full-year losses were expected to decline to 100-180 billion won from a 246 billion loss a year ago on an improved national economy and increased domestic air fares.

"The won's depreciation against the dollar has caused huge foreign exchange translation losses, leading to a deterioration in the company's overall business performance," said Choi Young-ho, an airline analyst at Ssangyong Securities.
He said the dollar had strengthened to 830-890 won so far this year against a 780-830 won range a year earlier.
Analysts said a one percentage point fluctuation in exchange rates cost Korean Air tens of billions of won.

They said Korean Air's extensive use of the dollar in plane purchases and borrowings increased its financing costs in won terms. Its liabilities totalled about 5.7 trillion won last year, half of which were borrowed in dollars, Choi said.
"Their business operations were not good either during the first half due to the sluggish economy and air fare discounts," said Jee Heon-seok, senior analyst at Daewoo Securities.
"The company needs to more aggressively hedge against its foreign exchange losses," he added.

Analysts said an increase in depreciation costs also contributed to the company's loss. Jee said Korean Air's depreciation cost would rise to 700 billion won this year from 685.5 billion in 1996 and 500 billion in 1995.

But analysts said a recent stabilising trend in foreign exchange rates and oil prices, as well as a rising load factor, would combine to improve the company's business earnings despite the plane crash.
"Korean tourists are not likely to switch to foreign airlines. They prefer the nation's airlines due to language and more familiar services," Choi said.

But a foreign securities house analyst who asked not to be identified said the crash was negative. "The accident is a very negative factor. Korean Air is known as one of the riskier airlines to foreign passengers, in particular, who are keen on safety.

Marty Salfen, senior vice president of the International Airline Passengers Association, said Korean Air had a relatively high accident rate of 1.91 per million departures over the past 10 years, against the world-wide rate of 0.581 per million.
The figure does not include the loss of KAL flight 007, a Boeing 747 that strayed into Soviet airspace in 1983 and was shot down. All 269 people aboard died.
(Conversion $1 = 890.00 won)
